documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT VISIT

66-year-old woman moving her primary care here; she wanted a practice where she can reach the physician directly. Long list, but she knows it cold and brought a typed medication sheet.

Myasthenia gravis, generalized. Thymectomy 2005. On pyridostigmine 60 mg three times a day, which she times around meals. Followed once a year by an outside neurology clinic. No current ptosis, double vision or swallowing trouble.

Multiple sclerosis, relapsing-remitting, same neurology clinic. Main day-to-day issue is the neurogenic bladder: she self-catheterizes several times a day and has had a number of urinary infections over the years, treated by her old practice. Gets catheters through a mail-order supplier.

COPD, described to her as moderate. Former smoker, about 15 pack-years, quit in the mid-1990s. Takes theophylline ER 200 mg twice daily, long-standing. Walks the dog every day without stopping.

Hypertension on HCTZ 25 mg. Knee osteoarthritis both sides, scoped in 2015, uses acetaminophen 500 mg when the knees ache. Osteopenia on a DXA last year; takes vitamin D3 2000 units and calcium carbonate 500 mg twice daily.

PSH: thymectomy 2005, diagnostic knee arthroscopy 2015, appendectomy long ago.
Allergies: none known.
Family: mother had breast cancer at 65. Father had COPD and high blood pressure. Sister has MS. Paternal grandmother broke a hip from osteoporosis.
Social: married, lives in Hadley. Retired elementary school teacher, now a part-time archivist at a library. A glass or two of wine a week. Former smoker as above.
Gyn: menopause around 2012, no bleeding since, never took hormones.

ROS: no chest pain, no change in breathing, no weight change, no bowel change. Negative otherwise.

Exam: vitals as charted. Pleasant, articulate. No ptosis; extraocular movements full. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement. Heart regular without murmur. Lungs with slightly reduced air movement at the bases, no wheeze. Abdomen soft, healed scars. Knees with crepitus both sides, no effusion today. Strength full in arms and legs, gait steady. Mood bright. PHQ-2 0.

Assessment and plan
1. Myasthenia gravis, MS with neurogenic bladder: stable; continue pyridostigmine; will request neurology notes.
2. COPD: stable on theophylline; level today. Requesting prior spirometry.
3. Hypertension: reasonable today on HCTZ; BMP.
4. Knee OA: acetaminophen as needed.
5. Osteopenia: continue calcium and D; DXA timing once the old report is in hand.
6. Health maintenance: hep C screen today; will pull prior colonoscopy, mammogram and vaccine records. Flu shot when the high-dose arrives.

Records release signed for prior primary care. Follow up 6 months, sooner as needed.

Neurology Clinic — Follow-up Letter
Date of visit: 03/14/2019

Dear Colleague,

Thank you for taking over Mrs. Kenney's primary care. I saw her today for her yearly review of generalized myasthenia gravis (post-thymectomy) and relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.

Myasthenia: no fluctuating weakness, diplopia, dysarthria or swallowing difficulty since last year. On examination there is no ptosis with sustained upgaze, and neck flexion and limb strength are full without fatigability.

MS: no new neurological symptoms and no relapse this year. Bladder managed with clean intermittent catheterization.

Plan: pyridostigmine 60 mg three times daily, unchanged. Please keep in mind that several antibiotic classes (fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides) and magnesium can worsen myasthenia. Review in 12 months.

Neurology Clinic

Orthopedic Surgery — Outpatient Consultation
Date of service: 07/01/2019
Referred by: primary care

Reason: bilateral knee pain.

History: 67-year-old woman with half a year of steadily increasing pain in both knees, aggravated by activity and worst by the end of the day, rated 7 of 10 on most days. Six weeks of physical therapy and an effort at weight loss have not given meaningful relief. She is clear that she does not want opioid pain medicine and would like options that keep her walking her dog every day, which matters a great deal to her. Takes acetaminophen as needed. Background of myasthenia gravis, MS with neurogenic bladder, COPD, hypertension and osteopenia. Arthroscopy for diagnosis in 2015.

Medications: pyridostigmine, theophylline, hydrochlorothiazide, acetaminophen as needed, vitamin D3, calcium carbonate.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: vital signs normal. Both knees with palpable crepitus and a small effusion; no warmth or redness. Range of motion mildly limited by pain at end flexion. Ligaments intact.

Imaging: standing films of both knees show medial joint-space narrowing with marginal osteophytes, no fracture.

Labs: ESR 20 mm/hr, CRP 1.2 mg/L, CBC within normal limits; no evidence of an inflammatory arthritis.

Impression: osteoarthritis of both knees.

Plan: after discussion of risks, each knee was injected with triamcinolone 40 mg and lidocaine under sterile technique, tolerated well. Continue acetaminophen and the home exercise program. May repeat injections no more often than every 3 months. Return as needed.

Orthopedic Surgery

documents.title: Office Visit — Fatigue and Fog
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Here six months after her orthopedics visit (knees much better since the injections). Now a few months of feeling worn out and achy all over, constipated, and "foggy" in a way she says isn't her. Loses her place at the archive and has trouble keeping a task in her head. Generally weaker, though she separates this from myasthenia: no droopy lids, no double vision, no trouble chewing. Drinking a lot more water and up to urinate more than usual between caths; no burning, no blood, urine looks clear. Eating less. Home scale went from about 70 kg in September to 66 now without trying. No fever, no night sweats, no cough beyond baseline. No new medications or supplements beyond her usual list.

Meds: pyridostigmine 60 TID, theophylline ER 200 BID, HCTZ 25 daily, acetaminophen PRN, vitamin D3 2000 units, calcium carbonate 500 BID.

O: T 36.7, P 76, BP 148/86. Weight 66.5 kg, BMI 25. Looks tired but well. Neuro: no ptosis, strength full and not fatigable, reflexes symmetric, no focal findings. Tender to pressure over both forearms and both shins. Heart regular. Lungs at baseline. Abdomen soft, nontender. Cognitive screen: slow on delayed recall (2 of 3 words, needed a cue for the third) and lost her place on serial 7s.

DXA from last week: osteopenia at spine, hip and forearm, forearm the lowest (T -2.3).

A/P: Fatigue, bone pain, constipation, polyuria and thirst, cognitive slowing and weight loss. Want calcium and PTH first; also check thyroid, B12, counts and liver tests.
- CMP, PTH, phosphorus, vitamin D, CBC, TSH, B12 today.
- BP higher than usual today; recheck once this is sorted out.
- Will call her with results tomorrow.

documents.title: Call — calcium and PTH results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Called pt with yesterday's results. Calcium 11.6 with albumin 4.1, intact PTH 128, phosphorus 2.3, vitamin D 32. CBC, TSH and B12 normal; kidney and liver tests fine.

High calcium with a PTH that is high rather than suppressed: primary hyperparathyroidism. Explained this likely accounts for the fatigue, aches, thirst, constipation and fog, and probably the forearm bone density. Next step is a 24-hour urine to finish the workup, then a surgical opinion. Advised plenty of fluids.

She will pick up the collection jug Monday and do the collection over the weekend after. Questions answered; she was relieved there is an explanation.

documents.title: 24-hour urine calcium — result and referral
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
24-hour urine calcium 310 mg, collection adequate by creatinine. Not low, so this is not familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia; it is primary hyperparathyroidism, and with symptoms, forearm bone loss and high urine calcium she meets criteria for surgery.

Called pt: explained, she would like to see a surgeon. Referral to endocrine surgery placed. Records sent: labs, DXA, med list. Flagged myasthenia for their anesthesia team.

Endocrine Surgery — New Patient Consultation
Date of service: 01/29/2020

Dear Doctor,

Thank you for sending Mrs. Kenney, a 68-year-old woman with primary hyperparathyroidism: calcium 11.6 mg/dL, intact PTH 128 pg/mL, phosphorus 2.3, 25-OH vitamin D 32, 24-hour urine calcium 310 mg. She describes several months of fatigue, aches, thirst, constipation and poor concentration. DXA shows osteopenia, lowest at the distal radius.

History also includes generalized myasthenia gravis after thymectomy in 2005, relapsing-remitting MS with neurogenic bladder, moderate COPD, hypertension and knee osteoarthritis. Medications: pyridostigmine, theophylline, hydrochlorothiazide, acetaminophen, vitamin D3, calcium carbonate. NKDA.

Exam: well appearing. Neck without palpable mass or thyroid nodule. Voice normal.

Imaging: Tc-99m sestamibi SPECT/CT on 01/21/2020 shows a single focus of persistent tracer uptake posterior to the lower pole of the left thyroid lobe, consistent with a left inferior parathyroid adenoma. No ectopic focus. Thyroid otherwise unremarkable.

Assessment: symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism with a single localized adenoma.

Plan: focused left neck exploration with intraoperative PTH monitoring, planned for February. Anesthesia aware of myasthenia; we will avoid or minimize neuromuscular blockade and she should take her morning pyridostigmine. Expect same-day discharge.

Endocrine Surgery

reports.text:
Specimen: left inferior parathyroid gland.
Gross: an ovoid tan-brown nodule, 0.9 g.
Microscopic: hypercellular parathyroid tissue composed predominantly of chief cells with a rim of compressed normal parathyroid; no capsular or vascular invasion; no atypia.

documents.title: Operative note — focused parathyroidectomy
documents.author: endocrine surgery
documents.body:
Operative Report
Date of surgery: 02/19/2020

Preoperative diagnosis: primary hyperparathyroidism, left inferior adenoma on sestamibi.
Procedure: minimally invasive left inferior parathyroidectomy with intraoperative PTH monitoring.
Anesthesia: general, no neuromuscular blocking agent; morning pyridostigmine given.

Findings: an enlarged left inferior parathyroid gland, 0.9 g, removed intact. Left superior gland normal in appearance and left in place. Recurrent laryngeal nerve identified and preserved.

Intraoperative PTH: 141 pg/mL before excision, 22 pg/mL at 10 minutes after excision.

Estimated blood loss minimal. No complications. Extubated in the operating room, strength at baseline in recovery. Discharged home the same afternoon. Frozen and final pathology: parathyroid adenoma.

Instructions: calcium carbonate as needed for tingling for 2 weeks, resume home medicines. Calcium check in 2 weeks with primary care.

Endocrine Surgery

Two weeks out from left inferior parathyroidectomy (adenoma, PTH fell from 141 to 22 in the OR). No tingling around the mouth or fingers, did not need the extra calcium. Thirst gone. Energy better, bowels back to normal, and she says the fog is lifting; back at the archive two mornings a week. Appetite up, weight coming back.

Exam: incision healing well, no swelling. Voice normal. No ptosis. Bones no longer tender.

Calcium today 9.4.

A/P: primary hyperparathyroidism cured by surgery; problem resolved. Continue her calcium carbonate and vitamin D for bone health. Repeat DXA in a few years to see whether the forearm improves. BP better today.

documents.title: Gynecology consultation
documents.author: gynecology
documents.body:
Gynecology — Consultation
Date of service: 06/29/2020 (addendum 07/03/2020)

Reason for referral: postmenopausal bleeding.

HPI: 68-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis after thymectomy and multiple sclerosis, recently treated for primary hyperparathyroidism, who has had about a month of light "pinkish" spotting, usually noticed after a bowel movement. No pelvic pain, discharge, urinary symptoms or trauma. Menopause 8 years ago with no bleeding since. No history of hormone replacement. Hypertension controlled; osteopenia.

Medications: pyridostigmine, theophylline, hydrochlorothiazide, acetaminophen, vitamin D3, calcium carbonate. NKDA.

Exam: external genitalia normal. Vaginal mucosa atrophic, no lesions. Cervix without lesions. Bimanual: uterus not enlarged; a firm left adnexal mass is palpable, mobile, nontender.

Ultrasound today: complex solid and cystic left ovarian mass measuring 7 cm; endometrium homogeneously thickened to 11 mm.

Labs: estradiol is above the postmenopausal range and FSH is suppressed, suggesting an estrogen-producing ovarian tumor.

Procedure: endometrial biopsy performed in the office with a pipelle, tolerated well; pathology pending.

Addendum 07/03: pelvic MRI 07/02 shows the mass confined to the left ovary, no extra-ovarian disease, no adenopathy.

Impression: complex left adnexal mass with hormonal evidence of estrogen production, most consistent with a sex cord-stromal tumor of the ovary; thickened endometrium.

Plan: referred to gynecologic oncology; biopsy result will go to them and to you.

Gynecology

documents.title: Gynecologic oncology consultation
documents.author: gynecologic oncology
documents.body:
Gynecologic Oncology — New Patient Consultation
Date of service: 07/09/2020

Mrs. Kenney is a 68-year-old woman referred for a 7 cm complex left ovarian mass found during evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding. Estradiol is elevated for age with a suppressed FSH. MRI shows the mass is confined to the left ovary.

Endometrial biopsy (06/29): proliferative endometrium. No hyperplasia or malignancy.

Background: generalized myasthenia gravis after thymectomy, relapsing-remitting MS with neurogenic bladder on intermittent catheterization, moderate COPD on theophylline, hypertension, and parathyroidectomy in February of this year. NKDA.

Exam: abdomen soft, no ascites. Pelvic: firm, mobile left adnexal mass about 7 cm. No nodularity.

Impression: presumed estrogen-secreting sex cord-stromal tumor of the left ovary, clinically confined to the ovary; granulosa cell tumor most likely.

Plan: total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and surgical staging, scheduled 07/28. Pre-operative medical evaluation with her primary care physician requested. Our anesthesia team is aware of her myasthenia; neurology will be informed.

Gynecologic Oncology

- Watch respiratory effort closely post-op given myasthenia and COPD; incentive spirometry.
- Theophylline: take the morning dose; resume when eating.
- HCTZ may be held the day of surgery.

Operative Report
Date of surgery: 07/28/2020

Preoperative diagnosis: left adnexal mass, suspected sex cord-stromal tumor.
Procedure: exploratory laparotomy, total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, pelvic washings, infracolic omentectomy, peritoneal biopsies.

Findings: 7 cm smooth left ovarian mass, capsule intact, no surface excrescences, no rupture. Right ovary and both tubes normal in appearance. Uterus normal size. Upper abdomen, diaphragm surfaces, liver and bowel without visible disease. No ascites. Frozen section: sex cord-stromal tumor, favor granulosa cell tumor.

Anesthesia: general; neuromuscular blockade avoided. Extubated in the operating room without difficulty.

Estimated blood loss 250 mL. No complications.

reports.text:
Specimens: uterus with cervix, bilateral tubes and ovaries; omentum; peritoneal biopsies; pelvic washings.
Left ovary: adult granulosa cell tumor, 7.0 cm, capsule intact, no surface involvement. Microscopic: diffuse and microfollicular growth of cells with grooved nuclei; Call-Exner bodies present. Inhibin and calretinin positive.
Right ovary and both fallopian tubes: no tumor.
Uterus: proliferative endometrium; no hyperplasia or carcinoma. Cervix unremarkable.
Omentum and peritoneal biopsies: no tumor.
Pelvic washings: negative for malignant cells.
reports.conclusion: Adult granulosa cell tumor of the left ovary, 7.0 cm, confined to the ovary with intact capsule. FIGO stage IA.

Arrival: 07/08/2022 19:15   Departure: 07/09/2022 09:40

Chief complaint: palpitations, nausea, feeling restless.

documents.author: critical care
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 07/10/2022 (medical ICU)   Discharged: 07/19/2022

Principal diagnosis: myasthenic crisis.
Other diagnoses: urinary tract infection, Proteus (diagnosed in our ED 07/06); theophylline toxicity (ED 07/08), resolved; COPD; hypertension; relapsing-remitting MS with neurogenic bladder; history of ovarian granulosa cell tumor and of parathyroid adenoma, both resected.

History: 70-year-old woman with generalized myasthenia gravis after thymectomy. On 07/06 she came to our ED with fever, chills, lower abdominal pain and cloudy, foul-smelling urine, with harder voiding despite her usual intermittent catheterization; she was tender over the bladder, urinalysis was alkaline with many white cells and crystals, an abdominal film showed no radiopaque stones, and she was sent home on ciprofloxacin. Culture grew Proteus. On 07/08 she returned with theophylline toxicity (level 25), theophylline was held and she went home the next morning. She came back 07/10 with two days of worsening breathlessness and weakness that began after the antibiotic was started.

On arrival: working to breathe with accessory muscles, speaking in short phrases. T 37.8 C, BP 145/90, HR 88, RR 26, SpO2 92% on room air. Bilateral ptosis and diplopia. Breath sounds diminished on both sides with a prolonged expiratory phase. Cough weak. Unable to raise her head from the pillow. ABG: pH 7.32, PaCO2 50, PaO2 70, HCO3 24.

Hospital course:
- Myasthenic crisis, likely provoked by ciprofloxacin in the setting of infection. Admitted to the ICU. BiPAP for 3 days; intubation was not needed. IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days. Pyridostigmine held while on BiPAP and restarted on hospital day 4 at 60 mg three times daily. Neurology followed daily. Neck and limb strength improved steadily; ptosis and diplopia resolved by day 6. Transferred to the floor day 5, worked with PT, walking the hall independently at discharge.
- UTI: ciprofloxacin stopped on admission; ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily to complete 7 days of treatment. Afebrile from day 2.
- Theophylline toxicity: theophylline kept on hold for the whole stay; no arrhythmia.
- Creatinine returned to her baseline.

Discharge medications: pyridostigmine 60 mg three times daily; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; acetaminophen 500 mg as needed; vitamin D3 2000 units daily; calcium carbonate 500 mg twice daily.
HELD: theophylline, pending review by her primary care physician.

Medications to avoid in myasthenia: fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides, IV magnesium, and others per neurology handout given to the patient.

Follow-up: primary care within 1 week; neurology 08/15/2022.

Critical Care Medicine

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD (with observation stay)
Arrival: 06/27/2026 11:20   Discharge: 06/28/2026 17:30

Chief complaint: memory loss and confusion.

History (mostly from husband): 74-year-old woman with generalized myasthenia gravis after thymectomy and relapsing-remitting MS. Over roughly two months she has become steadily more forgetful, asking the same question again and again in one conversation, and acting in ways that are out of character for her. Lately she has had trouble recognizing familiar people's faces and everyday objects. The husband brought her in today because it is getting worse week by week. No fever or headache reported. Previous episode of confusion was with hyperparathyroidism in 2019, treated surgically.

Medications: pyridostigmine 60 mg TID, theophylline ER 200 mg BID, acetaminophen PRN, vitamin D3, calcium carbonate. (Husband also reports hydrochlorothiazide for blood pressure.)
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: vitals as recorded, afebrile. Awake, disoriented to time and place, follows simple commands. Myoclonic jerks of both upper extremities, and an exaggerated startle to sudden noise. No meningismus. No ptosis. No focal weakness found.

Workup: CBC, CMP (including calcium), TSH and B12 normal. Urinalysis negative. MRI brain: diffuse cortical atrophy without stroke or mass; white-matter lesions of known MS. Lumbar puncture: CSF WBC 2, RBC 0, protein 45, glucose 60; Gram stain no organisms, culture no growth, HSV PCR negative; nothing to suggest an infectious or inflammatory encephalitis. Neurology consulted in the ED. EEG 06/28: generalized periodic triphasic sharp-wave complexes.

Neurology impression: rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus and periodic sharp waves on EEG; prion disease is the main concern. CSF sent for 14-3-3 protein.

Disposition: discharged home with husband under supervision, 06/28. Neurology clinic follow-up 07/23 for the CSF result. PCP follow-up this week. Return for fever, falls, inability to eat or drink, or worse confusion.

Emergency Medicine / Observation Unit

They did an MRI, a spinal tap and a brain wave test; the neurologist mentioned a possible prion disease and sent a special spinal fluid test, results in a few weeks. Neurology appointment 7/23.

documents.title: Office Visit — After ED Visit for Confusion
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen with husband, who gives most of the history. ED record not yet received; history from him and the discharge paperwork.

He dates the change to late April: forgetting conversations, repeating questions, then doing things that weren't like her. In the last weeks she has had trouble recognizing faces and objects, and her arms jerk. At the March wellness visit her Mini-Cog was normal and neither of them had concerns.

In the ER (6/27-28): labs normal including calcium, MRI with atrophy but no stroke or mass, spinal fluid without signs of infection, and an EEG with a periodic pattern. Neurology raised prion disease and sent a CSF 14-3-3.

Today she is pleasant, says she is "just tired," disoriented to the date and to where we are. Brief myoclonic jerks of both arms during the visit, and she startles at a door closing. No ptosis. Afebrile, vitals as charted.

Meds: unchanged; husband now sets out her pills.

Assessment: rapidly progressive cognitive decline with myoclonus. Neurology's working concern is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease; awaiting the CSF result and the 7/23 visit.

Plan
- Husband to supervise medicines; no driving; she should not be alone at home.
- Discussed with both what the concern is, as much as they wanted to hear today; he wants to wait for neurology before planning further.
- Proxy access to the portal set up for husband.
- Call with any fever, falls, swallowing trouble or sudden change.
- Will see after neurology.

Neurology Clinic — Follow-up
Date of service: 07/23/2026

Dear Colleague,

I saw Mrs. Kenney with her husband for follow-up of the rapidly progressive cognitive decline we first evaluated in the emergency department a month ago. She is 74 and has generalized myasthenia gravis (post-thymectomy) and relapsing-remitting MS.

History from her husband: about three months of memory loss and erratic behavior, now with difficulty walking and several episodes of sudden jerking. No recent travel and no sick contacts.

Exam: alert, disoriented to time and place. Myoclonic jerks of the upper limbs. Gait broad-based and unsteady. No ptosis or fatigable weakness.

Results: routine bloods from June normal. CSF from the June lumbar puncture: WBC 2, RBC 0, protein 45 mg/dL, glucose 60 mg/dL. CSF 14-3-3 protein: elevated. MRI from June shows no acute changes. EEG with generalized periodic sharp-wave complexes.

Impression: rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus, visual and cerebellar features, periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG and an elevated CSF 14-3-3: probable sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

Discussion and plan: I explained the diagnosis and its usual course to her husband, and that there is no treatment that slows or stops it. Care is supportive and centered on comfort, safety and support for him. I recommend palliative care involvement now, home safety measures and supervision at all times, and no driving. Myasthenia medicines unchanged. CJD is a reportable condition and I have notified the state public health department as required. Return in 6 weeks or sooner as needed.

Neurology Clinic
